newsitem.title: POLAND: OPINION - NOBE INSTITUTE POLISH QUARTERLY FORECAST.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - NOBE INSTITUTE POLISH QUARTERLY FORECAST.

text.p: Following is a quarterly macroeconomic forecast
commissioned by Reuters from Poland's Independent Centre for
Economic Research (NOBE).
Developments in the Polish economy in the second half of
1996 took a different turn from that predicted by forecasters.
The economy started to overheat. As a result, the trade
balance began to deteriorate quickly and some slowdown of
growth is unavoidable to restore equilibrium.
Implementing the right policy mix may be difficult in a
parliamentary election year. Close collaboration between the
National Bank of Poland (NBP) and the government will be vital
to avoid either an excessive economic slowdown or a surge in
inflation.
DISAPPOINTING EXPORTS COINCIDE WITH ROBUST DOMESTIC DEMAND
Poland's economic performance in the second half of 1996
was influenced mainly by four factors.
First, improvements in exports did not materialise, mainly
due to weaker-than-expected foreign demand, particularly in
Germany. At the same time, strong growth in domestic demand
maintained the high pace of imports growth. As a consequence,
the trade balance significantly deteriorated.
Second, rapid credit expansion triggered a fast rise in
disposable income and consumer demand.
Third, investment demand remained very high due to the
domestic credit expansion and the continuous inflow of foreign
direct investment.
Fourth, a clear overheating of the economy did not cause
inflationary effects but resulted in a widening trade deficit.
This was partly due to the central bank's crawling peg exchange
rate policy, which left little room for increases in the price
of goods.
It was also in part due to government efforts, including
delays in necessary adjustments of government-controlled
prices.
CAREFUL POLICY RESPONSE NEEDED
The economic situation now requires a careful policy
response which in our view should address the following issues:
1. External equilibrium.
The equilbrium should be seen in the context of the whole
balance of payments rather than only of the trade balance. As
the reserves level remains satisfactory, we do not think that
any drastic change in the exchange rate policy is necessary.
Poland's export performance should finally improve in 1997 when
West European growth accelerates. This factor, together with a
slower growth of import demand, should allow the trade balance
to stabilise at a level that can be safely financed through FDI
(foreign direct investment) and limited long-term borrowing.
2. Domestic demand.
Domestic absorption increased sharply in the third and
fourth quarters of 1996, growing by nine percent in the year.
Growth of individual consumption and gross fixed capital
formation was fuelled by a rapid expansion of domestic credit
(by about 15 percent in real terms).
The rapid increase in credit to households is generally
blamed for the fast growth of consumption. But we tend to
believe an increase in credit to firms, which is less
impressive in growth terms but three times larger in amount,
creates the greatest potential danger to economic stability.
The credit expansion should be slowed by a more effective
monetary policy, and mainly by higher real interest rates.
3. Interest rate policy and investment.
If the exchange rate policy is maintained, and after some
initial inflationary effects of administrative price
adjustments are absorbed, the inflation rate should continue to
fall, particularily in the second and third quarters of 1997.
That would allow real interest rates to grow without a need
for any drastic policy actions. Higher costs of credit,
combined with the greater uncertainty caused by the general
election, should result in a slowdown of investment. However,
if no drastic action is undertaken, the growth of investment
may increase again in the last months of 1997.
4. Fiscal policy and consumption.
Fiscal policy, particularly wage policy in the public
sector and the pension system, is likely to be under strong
political pressure in the second and third quarters of 1997. It
is crucial that no further relaxation of this policy takes
place. The NBP could try to limit expansion of credit for
households through moral persuasion, and use more radical tools
only if this fails. A cautious fiscal policy, supported by
growing real interest rates, should be enough to slow the
growth of real incomes and consumption.
GROWTH MAY SLOW IN Q3, FIVE PERCENT POSSIBLE FOR YEAR
Under the assumed economic policy we expect GDP growth to
slow to about four percent in the third quarter of 1997. For
the whole of 1997, growth of about five percent is possible.
The foreign trade deficit will be growing, but the gap between
the rates of exports and imports growth is likely to close by
the end of 1997. Producer price inflation, after some increase
in mid-1997, will fall again to 10 percent, while consumer
inflation will be falling steadily to about 14 percent.
Interest rate cuts are likely to be very modest.
The policy mix that we suggest does not include any drastic
change in the exchange rate, monetary, and fiscal policy.
Although the situation is delicate, we see no reasons for
panic. A cautious, carefully thought-out policy is likely to
cool down the economy to the necessary degree, while any
drastic action, particularily uncoordinated and executed in a
tense political environment, may lead to unexpected results.
